source_read: Publisher HTML (Wiley Online Library; Addiction editorial, free access, 2015;110:726-727), read in full in my own browser tab: italic standfirst (a blockquote, not counted as a paragraph), 10 paragraphs, declaration of interests and the 19-item reference list.

claims.note: An opinion editorial with no numbers and no systematic search. It supports the claim's comparison-group argument (stricter abstainer groups remove the apparent protection) and its 'disputed' status. Its own conclusion goes further than the claim (the protective hypothesis so undermined that burden estimates and guidelines should no longer assume any protection); the claim's 'evidence is insufficient' does not overstate it. Interests: declared none, but three of its six authors (Chikritzhs, Stockwell, Naimi) are authors of the 2016 analysis the claim cites (Stockwell et al. 2016; author list as printed in Griswold 2018, ref 28), and three of its 19 references are the editorial authors' own work (refs 5, 7, 8); the claim already says the 2016-2024 analyses come from one group. The Holmes et al. result is described for drinkers of 21 g a day or less, with the variant's protective association seen only among drinkers; the editorial says any mortality benefit would be driven by cardiovascular outcomes, which fits the claim's point that genetic studies concern heart disease rather than all-cause deaths.

anchors.extracted: Fillmore et al. (2006): longitudinal studies grouped by abstainer definition; those excluding former and occasional drinkers from the abstainer reference showed no significant protection from moderate drinking (sick-quitter mechanism). Liang and Chikritzhs (2013): former and current drinkers combined and compared with lifelong abstainers, plus confounder adjustment, removed the difference in health between abstainers and low-dose drinkers. No figures given.

Holmes et al. Mendelian randomisation meta-analysis: among people drinking 21 g a day or less, carriers of a variant linked to lower intake had fewer cardiovascular events, the association seen only in drinkers; HDL-C, CRP and fibrinogen may not be causal for CHD; any mortality benefit at low intake would be driven by cardiovascular outcomes.
Authors' opinion: the protective hypothesis is so undermined that burden-of-disease estimates (including GBD) and national guidelines should stop assuming any protection from low-dose drinking.

key_findings.correction: The summary line is an italic blockquote in the HTML, not a running paragraph, so the card's paragraph numbering (1st = 'For several decades...') matches the locator convention.
Reference titles checked: ref 11 is an NBER working paper on in-utero exposure and academic achievement; ref 12 a UK birth-cohort study of prenatal exposure and childhood balance.

reporting_issues.note: Agree it is ambiguous; in my blind reading I took the 21 g a day as a subgroup of the analysis, which is one of the two readings, so my anchor should not be used for that detail either.
The citations in that paragraph (refs 17, 18) belong to the preceding sentence on intima-media thickness and calcification.
Ref 3 'Ronksley R.'; refs 13 and 14 'Davey S. G.'; ref 16 'Dave S. G.'.
